architectural_implications.after: Versioned, diffable natural-language rule packs that domain owners and SMEs can read and amend, paired with MCP servers for capability.
architectural_implications.before: Agent workflows hard-coded in an orchestration framework, editable only by engineers who own the code.
architectural_implications.consequence: Faster process iteration and better human review of agent behavior, at the cost of relying on the model to faithfully interpret prose rules — interpretability replaces compile-time guarantees.
architectural_implications.observation: Orchestration policy is expressed as markdown rules and protocols in a repository rather than as framework code.

architectural_implications.after: Human approval gates the plan produced by research/leader agents before builder agents spend tokens.
architectural_implications.before: Human review happens at the end, on generated output or pull request.
architectural_implications.consequence: Cheaper rejection and a measurable human-attention bottleneck; the queue's throughput becomes the system's real throughput ceiling.
architectural_implications.observation: Human-in-the-loop approval is a queued stage in the pipeline between research and build.

architectural_implications.after: Modernization produces a mapped domain and a proposed agent-callable API surface, green-lit by product and tech before execution.
architectural_implications.before: Modernization produces code changes reviewed as patches.
architectural_implications.consequence: The API surface becomes the stable boundary agents operate against, which in turn makes legacy systems addressable by future agents — the mapping output is itself infrastructure.
architectural_implications.observation: Deliverables are agent-produced planning artifacts (domain maps, proposed agent-callable APIs) rather than only code diffs.

architectural_implications.after: Task-class routing where cheaper tiers handle legacy code reading/modification and expensive tiers are reserved where they empirically add value.
architectural_implications.before: A single frontier model used uniformly across all agent stages.
architectural_implications.consequence: Requires maintaining an internal benchmark harness per task class; token cost becomes a tunable engineering parameter rather than a fixed budget line.
architectural_implications.observation: Model tier is selected per task class based on measured cost per successful outcome.

article_ideas.angle: Reframe the familiar 'AI coding productivity' narrative as a budget-allocation problem: show the 75/25 engineer-bandwidth split, argue that automating the already-fast stage is optimizing the wrong variable, and give a procedure for locating the outer-loop stage worth automating.
article_ideas.audience: Engineering leaders, platform architects, and AI-infrastructure teams deciding where to invest agentic tooling
article_ideas.based_on: organizations remain stuck in the outer loop (system, context, owners, dependencies, intent, review, deploy)
article_ideas.thesis: GenAI already collapsed inner-loop coding time, so additional agent capacity spent on generation is near-worthless; the measurable leverage is in outer-loop stages — context acquisition, ownership mapping, dependency discovery, intent capture, and review/deploy coordination. Teams should instrument end-to-end lead time first and then point their agent fleet at whichever outer-loop stage owns the largest share, and should expect human approval queues, not models, to be the residual bottleneck.
article_ideas.title: Your Agents Are Fast; Your Org Is Slow: Aim Agent Fleets at the Outer Loop

article_ideas.angle: Architecture-with-economics: compare gate-before-build vs. review-after-generation cost profiles, and argue the gate should be designed as a loadable queue with measurable throughput rather than as an informal review habit.
article_ideas.audience: Agent platform engineers, DevEx and release-engineering teams, engineering managers running AI adoption
article_ideas.based_on: Human-in-the-loop approval is a queued stage in the pipeline between research and build.
article_ideas.thesis: Human review placed after generation is the most expensive possible place for a human to say no. Positioning approval as a queued stage between research/planning and execution means rejections cost a plan instead of a build, but it converts machine parallelism into human serialization — so the approval queue becomes the system's actual throughput ceiling and must be treated as an instrumented service with time-to-approval, rejection rate, and invalidated-work metrics.
article_ideas.title: Put the Human Gate Before the Build, Not After the Diff

article_ideas.angle: A concrete decomposition pattern with its failure modes: policy layer (diffable prose), capability layer (tool servers), and the missing third layer — enforcement verification — that determines whether prose-as-policy is safe.
article_ideas.audience: Architects designing multi-agent systems, MCP tooling authors, platform engineers
article_ideas.based_on: A markdown-based protocol and rule engine that breaks down large goals
article_ideas.thesis: Encoding multi-agent process — who may act, in what order, with what handoffs — as versioned markdown rule packs rather than orchestration framework code lets domain SMEs review and amend agent behavior directly and lets process change without a deploy; MCP servers keep tool capability a separate reusable substrate. The price is that interpretability replaces compile-time guarantees, so rule packs need conformance tests and violation telemetry to be trustworthy at scale.
article_ideas.title: Rules in Markdown, Capability in Servers: Separating Agent Policy From Agent Tooling

article_ideas.angle: Contrarian adoption argument: use the amplification claim as a diagnostic, propose a pre-flight process-health check before standing up an agent fleet, and redefine 'success' for a first mission around artifacts that reduce outer-loop ambiguity.
article_ideas.audience: Engineering directors, transformation leads, teams piloting agentic modernization
article_ideas.based_on: AI doesn't fix a team; it amplifies what's already there.
article_ideas.thesis: Agent fleets multiply whatever process quality already exists, so adopting them on a team with unresolved ownership, dependency, and intent ambiguity accelerates existing dysfunction rather than fixing it. The corollary is that the deliverable of a first war-room run should be judged on whether it produced durable shared understanding — a domain map, a proposed API boundary, named owners — and not on diff volume shipped.
article_ideas.title: Amplification, Not Repair: What Agent Fleets Actually Do to a Team

connections.relationship: Justifies pointing multi-agent capacity at context acquisition, ownership mapping, and review/deploy coordination rather than at code generation.
Clean split between process policy (natural-language, human-reviewable) and tool capability (servers); policy changes require no code deploy.
The human gate is a serialization point that sets the ceiling on builder-agent parallelism.

connections.concept: cost per request vs field match success
connections.relationship: Per-task-class benchmark becomes the routing table deciding which model tier serves which agent stage.

connections.connects_to: human attention as the scarce resource
connections.relationship: Naming drivers, SMEs, and decision-makers makes human attention allocatable and measurable alongside agent capacity.

evidence_quotes.text: Discusses how coding velocity in the inner loop has accelerated with genAI, but organizations remain stuck in the outer loop (system, context, owners, dependencies, intent, review, deploy)
We broke free of the outer loop; now it's your turn!

core_insights.generalization: For any agentic software system, measure where wall-clock time actually goes end-to-end before choosing which stage to automate; the highest-leverage agent work is usually in the unglamorous coordination stages.
core_insights.insight: The binding constraint on delivery is the outer loop (system context, ownership, dependencies, intent, review, deploy), not coding speed — and agent fleets must be aimed at that outer loop rather than at the inner-loop edit cycle where genAI already produced gains.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It relocates where an agentic system's value budget should be spent: on context acquisition, ownership mapping, and review/deploy coordination, not on code generation throughput. A team optimizing token spend on autocomplete-level tasks is optimizing the already-fast part.

evidence_quotes.text: A markdown-based protocol and rule engine that breaks down large goals, dispatches leader agents for research, queues human-in-the-loop approvals, and dispatches builder agents.
A structured collection of rules, protocols, markdown instructions, and MCP servers optimized for code modernization.

core_insights.generalization: Separate agent policy/process definition (versioned natural-language rule packs) from agent capability (tool servers) so process changes don't require redeploying orchestration code and domain experts can review the policy directly.
core_insights.insight: FleetKit encodes the multi-agent orchestration in a markdown-based rule/protocol layer plus MCP servers, with an explicit phase split: leader agents do research, a human-in-the-loop queue gates approval, then builder agents execute. The orchestration policy lives in reviewable text artifacts, not in bespoke framework code.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Rules-as-markdown makes agent behavior diffable, reviewable, and editable by the humans who own the domain, while MCP servers keep tool access as a separate, reusable substrate. It decouples policy (who may do what, in what order) from capability (what tools exist).

evidence_quotes.text: queues human-in-the-loop approvals, and dispatches builder agents
Incorporate human-in-the-loop (HITL) gates at critical milestones in automated workflows.

core_insights.generalization: In long-running agent workflows, insert human gates at the cheapest irreversible-decision boundary (plan approval) rather than at output review, and treat the gate as a queue with measurable throughput.
core_insights.insight: Human approval is modeled as a first-class queueing primitive positioned between the research phase and the build phase, rather than as a review step after generation.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Placing the gate before expensive build work changes the cost profile: humans reject bad plans before tokens are spent executing them, and the queue becomes an observable, loadable runtime component with its own latency and backlog characteristics.

evidence_quotes.text: a multi-player war room combining human decision-makers, drivers, subject matter experts (SMEs), and AI agent fleets working together
Roles mapped across comms channels, interactive design studios, code repositories, and agent automation suites.

core_insights.generalization: Design multi-agent systems by co-specifying human roles and agent roles with explicit handoff artifacts and channels; the human attention budget is the real constraint to optimize around.
core_insights.insight: The war room is a joint human-agent role decomposition, not just an agent topology: decision-makers, drivers, and SMEs are assigned alongside agent fleets across channels, design studios, repos, and the agent automation suite.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Most multi-agent designs specify only agent roles and leave the human attentional structure implicit, which produces undefined handoffs. Making human roles explicit turns the system into a schedulable organization where human attention is the scarce resource being allocated.

evidence_quotes.text: Benchmarks showed Claude Sonnet 5.5 performed just as well as (if not better than) Opus on legacy code modification tasks.
Comparative benchmarks on cost per request versus field match success rate.

core_insights.generalization: Benchmark each task class in your pipeline independently on cost-per-successful-outcome; expect heterogeneous model tiers to win across different stages (research vs. build vs. mapping).
core_insights.insight: Model selection was benchmarked per task class on cost per request versus task success, and the cheaper tier matched or beat the flagship on legacy code modification — suggesting legacy comprehension/modification is not where top-tier model capability is binding.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Directly changes token budget allocation: defaulting to the flagship model for bulk code-reading and modification work may be pure waste. It implies a routing policy keyed to task class rather than a single global model.

evidence_quotes.text: GEICO found engineers spent only 25% of their time on major strategic work versus minor patches and maintenance.
AI agents must be deployed to offload minor work and redirect engineering bandwidth to major work.

core_insights.generalization: Define automation targets by measuring the low-value fraction of human effort first, then build agents against that measured bucket rather than against nominal task volume.
core_insights.insight: The system was validated on an outcome metric that is a time reallocation, not a throughput metric: quantifying that engineers spent 75% of bandwidth on minor patches and upgrades defines the target of automation as recovering that bandwidth for major strategic work.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Choosing reallocated engineer-hours as the success metric changes what you build and how you justify it; it also makes agent output quality secondary to agent reliability on low-stakes repetitive work.

evidence_quotes.text: queues human-in-the-loop approvals, and dispatches builder agents
Incorporate human-in-the-loop (HITL) gates at critical milestones in automated workflows.
Every gate converts machine parallelism into human serialization; approval queues can become the dominant latency term in the pipeline.

deep_dives.research_question: When a human approval gate is placed between research and build phases, does the approval queue's latency and rejection rate dominate end-to-end wall-clock time compared to agent execution time, and how does gate placement (pre-build plan approval vs. post-build output review) change total token cost per accepted change?
deep_dives.topic: Human-in-the-loop approval queues as the real throughput ceiling in agent fleets
deep_dives.trigger_insight: queues human-in-the-loop approvals, and dispatches builder agents
deep_dives.why: The architecture makes human attention a runtime component with its own backlog. If the gate is the bottleneck, then investing in faster agents or cheaper models yields diminishing returns, and the engineering budget should shift to gate ergonomics, batch approval, and rejection-feedback loops. Without queue instrumentation, teams will misattribute slowness to models.

evidence_quotes.text: A markdown-based protocol and rule engine that breaks down large goals, dispatches leader agents for research, queues human-in-the-loop approvals, and dispatches builder agents.
A structured collection of rules, protocols, markdown instructions, and MCP servers optimized for code modernization.
interpretability replaces compile-time guarantees

deep_dives.research_question: Do agent behaviors specified as versioned markdown rule packs achieve equal or better task consistency and defect rate than equivalent behaviors encoded in orchestration framework code, and how often do models misinterpret prose rules in ways that produce silent policy violations?
deep_dives.topic: Prose-as-policy: markdown rule packs vs. compiled orchestration code
deep_dives.trigger_insight: A markdown-based protocol and rule engine that breaks down large goals
deep_dives.why: Moving orchestration policy into natural-language artifacts buys human reviewability and no-deploy iteration but trades away compile-time guarantees. Quantifying the misinterpretation rate turns a philosophical tradeoff into a measurable engineering parameter, and determines whether rule packs need conformance tests or a linting layer.

evidence_quotes.text: Benchmarks showed Claude Sonnet 5.5 performed just as well as (if not better than) Opus on legacy code modification tasks.
Comparative benchmarks on cost per request versus field match success rate.
The parity result is a vendor/product-specific benchmark on cost per request versus field match success rate; it may not transfer to other codebases, languages, or task shapes.

deep_dives.research_question: Across pipeline stages (domain mapping, API proposal, code modification, plan synthesis), does a cheaper model tier match a flagship tier on cost-per-successful-outcome, and is the winning tier stable across codebases and task shapes or specific to the reported benchmark harness?
deep_dives.topic: Per-task-class model routing economics for legacy code work
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Benchmarks showed Claude Sonnet 5.5 performed just as well as (if not better than) Opus on legacy code modification tasks.
deep_dives.why: A single global model choice is the default failure mode. If the cheap tier wins on bulk legacy reading and modification but loses on planning or API synthesis, then routing tables rather than model upgrades are the savings lever. The result reported is internally benchmarked and needs external replication to be trusted.

evidence_quotes.text: used $1,000 in AI tokens and one day to map a legacy domain, propose agent-callable APIs, and ship to UAT
the mapping output is itself infrastructure
Define coverage and correctness criteria for an agent-produced domain map (entry points, data dependencies, ownership boundaries) and measure agreement with SME-authored ground truth.

deep_dives.research_question: What coverage and correctness criteria can grade an agent-produced legacy domain map (entry points, data dependencies, ownership boundaries) and a proposed agent-callable API surface against SME-authored ground truth, and does map quality predict downstream build success?
deep_dives.topic: Agent-produced domain maps and API surfaces as first-class, evaluable artifacts
deep_dives.why: The mapping and API proposal are framed as the durable output of the mission — infrastructure rather than documentation. If that claim holds, map quality is a leading indicator of whether builder agents can execute at all, and it needs a metric independent of code-diff review. Otherwise mapping is unverifiable prose that reviewers rubber-stamp.

evidence_quotes.text: How to better handle prompt caching costs at scale?
Token cost behavior under sustained multi-agent fleet usage is unresolved by the team itself; the $1,000 one-day figure may not extrapolate to continuous operation.

deep_dives.research_question: How does marginal token cost per completed unit of work scale with shared rule-pack size, context reuse across leader and builder agents, and prompt-cache hit rate when a fleet runs continuously rather than for a single day?
deep_dives.topic: Token cost curves under continuous fleet operation and prompt-cache reuse
deep_dives.trigger_insight: How to better handle prompt caching costs at scale?
deep_dives.why: The one-day, $1,000 figure is the headline but is a bounded-burst number. Whether the approach is economically viable as a standing capability depends on cache hit rates and the marginal cost of replayed rule packs, which the team itself flags as unresolved. This determines if war rooms are a sprint tactic or an operating model.

project_ideas.based_on: queues human-in-the-loop approvals, and dispatches builder agents
project_ideas.hypothesis: In a leader/builder agent pipeline, end-to-end wall-clock time is dominated by human approval-queue latency and rejection-driven rework rather than by agent execution or token throughput; moving the gate from post-build review to pre-build plan approval reduces total token cost per accepted change by a measurable margin at equal or better change quality.
project_ideas.measurement: Tokens per accepted change, wall-clock breakdown by stage (agent vs. human queue), approval rejection rate, and fraction of build work discarded per rejection, across both variants on identical missions.
project_ideas.name: GateBench: Measuring the Human Gate, Not the Agent
project_ideas.poc: Build a two-variant harness over a small legacy repo: variant A runs research → build → human review on generated diffs; variant B runs research → human plan approval → build. Instrument both with time-to-approval, rejection rate, tokens spent per rejected plan, tokens spent per accepted change, and builder work invalidated per rejection.

project_ideas.based_on: A markdown-based protocol and rule engine that breaks down large goals
project_ideas.hypothesis: Markdown rule packs drive agent behavior with a measurable and bounded misinterpretation rate, and a lightweight conformance-test layer (canonical mission scenarios with expected policy outcomes) detects prose-policy violations that ad-hoc prompting would silently miss.
project_ideas.measurement: Policy-violation rate per scenario suite, run-to-run behavioral variance, and blast radius (number of scenarios changing outcome) per single-rule edit, for rule-pack vs. ad-hoc-prompt conditions.
project_ideas.name: RulePack Conformance Harness
project_ideas.poc: Author a small rule pack (phase split, tool permissions, handoff artifacts), then run a suite of scenario probes that should trigger specific policy decisions. Compare violation rate against an equivalent ad-hoc prompt baseline on the same scenarios, and diff behavior after an edit to a single rule to see whether changes are local or produce cascading drift.

project_ideas.based_on: Benchmarks showed Claude Sonnet 5.5 performed just as well as (if not better than) Opus on legacy code modification tasks.
project_ideas.hypothesis: The cost-optimal model tier differs by pipeline stage — a cheaper tier matches a flagship on legacy code reading and bulk modification while the flagship retains an edge on domain mapping and API-surface synthesis — so a static per-stage routing table beats uniform flagship use on cost per successful outcome at no quality loss.
project_ideas.measurement: Cost per successful outcome by stage and tier; quality delta per stage with confidence intervals on field-match success and downstream reviewer acceptance; total mission cost under routed vs. uniform-flagship deployment.
project_ideas.name: TierRouter: Per-Stage Model Routing on Cost per Successful Outcome
project_ideas.poc: Assemble a graded task set spanning four stages (code comprehension, bulk modification, domain mapping, API proposal) with field-match success criteria per stage. Run each stage under both tiers, log cost per request, and fit a small router that dispatches each stage to its cheapest non-inferior tier.

project_ideas.hypothesis: Agent-produced legacy domain maps and proposed agent-callable API surfaces can be graded against SME-authored ground truth on coverage and correctness, and map quality score predicts downstream build success (approval rate of migration plans, defect escape rate) better than map size or detail does.
project_ideas.measurement: Coverage and correctness score versus SME ground truth; correlation between map score and downstream plan-approval rate, builder rework, and defect escape rate to UAT.
project_ideas.name: MapScore: Grading Agent-Produced Domain Maps
project_ideas.poc: Take one bounded legacy domain, have SMEs author a reference map (entry points, data dependencies, ownership boundaries, callable operations). Produce agent maps under several prompting/rule-pack conditions, score them differentially against the reference, then run builder agents on each map and track plan approval and defects to UAT.

source.title: One Day, $1,000 in Tokens: An AI War Room for Legacy Code — Ford Prior, GEICO

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Ford Prior
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Building and running multi-player AI-native war rooms for legacy code modernization at GEICO using FleetKit.
  • Purpose: To share GEICO's practical experiment and framework (FleetKit and multi-player AI-native war rooms) for modernizing legacy codebases with AI agents while keeping human engineers focused on major work. Ford Prior from GEICO discusses how their claims engineering group tackled modernizing millions of lines of legacy code using an AI-native multi-player war room setup called FleetKit. With a budget of $1,000 in AI tokens and one day, they successfully mapped legacy domains, proposed agent-callable APIs, and shipped changes to UAT, proving that breaking free of the outer loop via multi-player AI war rooms can drastically accelerate software delivery.

Topic Map

The Outer Loop vs Inner Loop in SDLC

  • Explanation: Discusses how coding velocity in the inner loop has accelerated with genAI, but organizations remain stuck in the outer loop (system, context, owners, dependencies, intent, review, deploy).
  • Key claims:
    • AI doesn't fix a team; it amplifies what's already there.
    • Engineers spend only 25% of their time on major work.
  • Examples:
    • GEICO engineers spending 75% of bandwidth on minor patches and upgrades.
  • Terminology:
    • inner loop
    • outer loop
    • semantic versioning
  • Why it matters: Illustrates why engineering teams need collaboration and intelligence outside the coding phase to actually move faster.

The Multi-Player AI-Native War Room

  • Explanation: Introduces GEICO's solution: a multi-player war room combining human decision-makers, drivers, subject matter experts (SMEs), and AI agent fleets working together.
  • Key claims:
    • Major changes require deep collaboration and intelligence.
    • An AI war room bridges the gap between decision-makers and AI agents.
  • Examples:
    • Roles mapped across comms channels, interactive design studios, code repositories, and agent automation suites.
  • Terminology:
    • war room
    • driver
    • subject matter expert
    • agent fleet
  • Why it matters: Provides a structural approach to orchestrating multiple human and AI agents for enterprise-scale legacy changes.

The $1,000 One-Day Experiment (FleetKit)

  • Explanation: Details the experiment where GEICO used $1,000 in AI tokens and one day to map a legacy domain, propose agent-callable APIs, and ship to UAT.
  • Key claims:
    • Complex legacy systems can be mapped and modernized rapidly with proper AI tooling.
    • FleetKit turns Claude from a canvas into a factory.
  • Examples:
    • Uplift (Rentals), Transform (Damages), and Reimagine (Salvage) code-mod missions.
  • Terminology:
    • FleetKit
    • Fable
    • Claude Code Session
    • MCP servers
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates the practical feasibility and ROI of AI-driven legacy code modernization.

Key Points

Engineer time misallocation

  • Explanation: GEICO found engineers spent only 25% of their time on major strategic work versus minor patches and maintenance.
  • Evidence: Internal backlog analysis across 32 pizza teams.
  • Practical implication: AI agents must be deployed to offload minor work and redirect engineering bandwidth to major work.

FleetKit architecture

  • Explanation: A structured collection of rules, protocols, markdown instructions, and MCP servers optimized for code modernization.
  • Evidence: Used across rentals, damages, and salvage code-mod missions.
  • Practical implication: Transforms AI coding assistants into a scalable software factory.

Model selection insights

  • Explanation: Benchmarks showed Claude Sonnet 5.5 performed just as well as (if not better than) Opus on legacy code modification tasks.
  • Evidence: Comparative benchmarks on cost per request versus field match success rate.
  • Practical implication: Optimizes token spend without sacrificing output quality.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

FleetKit

  • How it works: A markdown-based protocol and rule engine that breaks down large goals, dispatches leader agents for research, queues human-in-the-loop approvals, and dispatches builder agents.
  • Components:
    • FleetKit repository
    • Claude Code Session (Fable)
    • Mission channel
    • Worksheets
    • HITL queue
  • When to use: When orchestrating multi-agent software engineering tasks on legacy enterprise codebases.

Examples & Case Studies

GEICO ran code-mod missions across Rentals, Damages, and Salvage domains.

  • Illustrates: Applying AI agent fleets to legacy code upgrade tasks.
  • Lesson: Salvage domain migration found a production bug and produced fully vetted migration plans green-lit by product and tech teams.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Adopt multi-player war room structures for complex software changes.
    • Use structured markdown rule kits (like FleetKit) to guide AI agent behavior.
  • Strategic:
    • Redirect engineering talent toward major strategic work by automating minor patches with AI agents.
    • Incorporate human-in-the-loop (HITL) gates at critical milestones in automated workflows.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How to better handle prompt caching costs at scale?
    • How to integrate audio transcription seamlessly as a data source for war rooms?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • GEICO has 300 engineers in 32 pizza teams with tech and business counterparts. (organizational structure)
  • Sonnet 5.5 performed as well as Opus on legacy code reading benchmarks. (benchmark performance)

Notable Quotes

"AI doesn't fix a team; it amplifies what's already there." "We broke free of the outer loop; now it's your turn!" (at 30:27)

Compressed Summary

  • Engineers spend only 25% of time on major work.
  • Multi-player AI war rooms combine human experts with agent fleets.
  • FleetKit turns AI models into a structured software factory.
  • Sonnet 5.5 matched Opus performance for legacy code modification at lower cost.
  • Keywords: fleetkit, legacy, modernization, agents, warroom

## Overview
- **Speaker**: Ford Prior
- **Channel**: AI Engineer
- **Main topic**: Building and running multi-player AI-native war rooms for legacy code modernization at GEICO using FleetKit.
- **Purpose**: To share GEICO's practical experiment and framework (FleetKit and multi-player AI-native war rooms) for modernizing legacy codebases with AI agents while keeping human engineers focused on major work.
Ford Prior from GEICO discusses how their claims engineering group tackled modernizing millions of lines of legacy code using an AI-native multi-player war room setup called FleetKit. With a budget of $1,000 in AI tokens and one day, they successfully mapped legacy domains, proposed agent-callable APIs, and shipped changes to UAT, proving that breaking free of the outer loop via multi-player AI war rooms can drastically accelerate software delivery.
## Topic Map
### The Outer Loop vs Inner Loop in SDLC
- **Explanation**: Discusses how coding velocity in the inner loop has accelerated with genAI, but organizations remain stuck in the outer loop (system, context, owners, dependencies, intent, review, deploy).
- **Key claims**:
  - AI doesn't fix a team; it amplifies what's already there.
  - Engineers spend only 25% of their time on major work.
- **Examples**:
  - GEICO engineers spending 75% of bandwidth on minor patches and upgrades.
- **Terminology**:
  - inner loop
  - outer loop
  - semantic versioning
- **Why it matters**: Illustrates why engineering teams need collaboration and intelligence outside the coding phase to actually move faster.
### The Multi-Player AI-Native War Room
- **Explanation**: Introduces GEICO's solution: a multi-player war room combining human decision-makers, drivers, subject matter experts (SMEs), and AI agent fleets working together.
- **Key claims**:
  - Major changes require deep collaboration and intelligence.
  - An AI war room bridges the gap between decision-makers and AI agents.
- **Examples**:
  - Roles mapped across comms channels, interactive design studios, code repositories, and agent automation suites.
- **Terminology**:
  - war room
  - driver
  - subject matter expert
  - agent fleet
- **Why it matters**: Provides a structural approach to orchestrating multiple human and AI agents for enterprise-scale legacy changes.
### The $1,000 One-Day Experiment (FleetKit)
- **Explanation**: Details the experiment where GEICO used $1,000 in AI tokens and one day to map a legacy domain, propose agent-callable APIs, and ship to UAT.
- **Key claims**:
  - Complex legacy systems can be mapped and modernized rapidly with proper AI tooling.
  - FleetKit turns Claude from a canvas into a factory.
- **Examples**:
  - Uplift (Rentals), Transform (Damages), and Reimagine (Salvage) code-mod missions.
- **Terminology**:
  - FleetKit
  - Fable
  - Claude Code Session
  - MCP servers
- **Why it matters**: Demonstrates the practical feasibility and ROI of AI-driven legacy code modernization.
## Key Points
### Engineer time misallocation
- **Explanation**: GEICO found engineers spent only 25% of their time on major strategic work versus minor patches and maintenance.
- **Evidence**: Internal backlog analysis across 32 pizza teams.
- **Practical implication**: AI agents must be deployed to offload minor work and redirect engineering bandwidth to major work.
### FleetKit architecture
- **Explanation**: A structured collection of rules, protocols, markdown instructions, and MCP servers optimized for code modernization.
- **Evidence**: Used across rentals, damages, and salvage code-mod missions.
- **Practical implication**: Transforms AI coding assistants into a scalable software factory.
### Model selection insights
- **Explanation**: Benchmarks showed Claude Sonnet 5.5 performed just as well as (if not better than) Opus on legacy code modification tasks.
- **Evidence**: Comparative benchmarks on cost per request versus field match success rate.
- **Practical implication**: Optimizes token spend without sacrificing output quality.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### FleetKit
- **How it works**: A markdown-based protocol and rule engine that breaks down large goals, dispatches leader agents for research, queues human-in-the-loop approvals, and dispatches builder agents.
- **Components**:
  - FleetKit repository
  - Claude Code Session (Fable)
  - Mission channel
  - Worksheets
  - HITL queue
- **When to use**: When orchestrating multi-agent software engineering tasks on legacy enterprise codebases.

### GEICO ran code-mod missions across Rentals, Damages, and Salvage domains.
- **Illustrates**: Applying AI agent fleets to legacy code upgrade tasks.
- **Lesson**: Salvage domain migration found a production bug and produced fully vetted migration plans green-lit by product and tech teams.

- **Immediate**:

  - Use structured markdown rule kits (like FleetKit) to guide AI agent behavior.
- **Strategic**:
